summary:
Trans visitors to Ghana face imprisonment for identity itself. The Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Ghana's Parliament on 29 May 2026 provides up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, with total prison terms of three to ten years and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Presidential assent by President John Mahama was still outstanding at the most recent reporting, and he had previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill.

The 2026 bill reaches beyond identity. Forming or funding an LGBTQ+ group carries up to five years; advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ+ activities carries three to five years, with some proposals at five to ten; public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people are also prohibited. A person who identifies publicly as an "ally" of LGBTQ people may also face prison.

A reporting duty compounds that exposure. The bill obliges anyone who becomes aware of prohibited acts to report them to the police, turning acquaintances, colleagues, landlords and hotel staff into potential informants and removing the ordinary discretion not to involve the authorities.

The bill's passage follows a cycle of failed enactment. A predecessor passed unanimously on third reading in February 2024, lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved before the 2024 election, and was reintroduced in March 2025 before passing again in May 2026. Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the 2024 bill, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson stating that until there is presidential assent there is no act and the review deferred until the president signs; the petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options.

Colonial-era law remains the standing basis for prosecution. Section 104(1)(b) of the Criminal Code 1960 criminalises "unnatural carnal knowledge" as a misdemeanour carrying up to three years. Enforcement overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people, while heterosexual couples performing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted; CDD-Ghana describes the practice as moral policing rather than criminal justice. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2018 that the provision is seldom used formally while documenting mob violence, police abuse and extortion, including 2017 victim interviews in Kumasi and Tamale.

No procedure for legal gender recognition or document change for transgender people is documented in these sources. The 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and Ghanaian law contains no broad protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment.

Venues that serve trans and LGBTQ visitors have been shut down rather than provided. The LGBTQ Centre in Accra was forced to close in February 2021 under pressure from religious and political leaders, and the office of LGBT+ Rights Ghana, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021. No publicly documented policy exists on housing trans prisoners, so the bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone without stating how such prisoners would be held.
tangentialFactors:
Constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech, expression and assembly exist on paper and are routinely denied to LGBTQ people in practice. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal.

Public opinion provides the political base for the legislation. In a 2017 ILGA poll, 89% of Ghanaians reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to the police, though 59% agreed that LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination, rising to 62% for transgender people, and 55% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate "unnatural sexual relations" and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all of the Committee's other recommendations at that review.

Political signals have been mixed. In January 2025 President John Mahama said he preferred teaching traditional family values through the school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, yet the 2026 bill was passed under pressure from religious leaders on a president whose ratification remained required. The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education.

Community organisations describe the current climate as one of panic and withdrawal. One Love Sisters Ghana reports eviction risk and self-censorship among members following the 2026 vote. A 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland found most opposed decriminalisation on religio-cultural grounds and effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBTQ relatives but not blessing their marriages; that study measures diaspora opinion rather than conditions inside Ghana.
localsOnly:
Healthcare is constrained by fear and by practitioner bias. Mental health professionals in Ghana are often not trained to work with LGBTQ populations and may hold prejudiced views, and the Ghana Mental Health Authority has not fully implemented inclusive policies under its 2012 Mental Health Act. Many LGBTQ people avoid seeking care altogether, creating barriers to mental and sexual health support.

Forced evictions, blackmail and violence are linked to anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and deaths by suicide. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana face significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers.

Conversion therapy is commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, frequently sought by families from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity. An August 2018 report documented conversion therapy programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed about 400 people had registered for such programmes. Medical bodies warn that conversion therapy is ineffective and potentially harmful.

Government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for heterosexual people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding.

Organised LGBTQ life operates underground. Most groups meet secretly or online, with members of FOTHA-Ghana using the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists; young LGBTQ people are disowned by families and communities and evicted from family homes. The Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.

Ghana does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and no provision of law allows legal recognition of same-sex relationships, leaving LGBTQ people in weak legal positions on long-term relationships and shared property. Same-sex couples are explicitly excluded from the adoption process because the system does not support joint applications from non-heterosexual partnerships. The 2026 bill would additionally ban same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples outright.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources contain no finding on legal gender recognition procedures or document-change rules for transgender people in Ghana. The nearest grounded items are the constitutional definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, Article 39's emphasis on traditional values, the 2017 ILGA poll figure of 55% support for legal gender change, and the bill's criminalisation of crossdressing and identifying as transgender. Whether any administrative route to a changed marker exists remains unresolved in this inventory.

Assent status is a live uncertainty. Reporting at the most recent dates states that President Mahama's signature was still required, but no source in this inventory confirms whether the bill has since been assented to, gazetted or brought into force, nor whether the deferred Supreme Court review has resumed.

No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners, and the sources do not describe how an imprisoned trans person would in practice be classified or held.

No sources address entry, visa or border-screening questions for Ghana, including whether passport markers, arrival cards or immigration interviews could disclose a visitor's gender identity or trans status. Nothing here should be read as an assurance that such screening is absent.

No sources address availability of hormone therapy, gender-affirming care or prescription continuity for visitors, nor the treatment of imported medication at the border.
